items.title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
items.summary: Hamas condemned the incursion, which the Israeli military said was to dismantle a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
items.content:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.

Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.

In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.

An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.

That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.

Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.

"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.

Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families

Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".

Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.

At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza

Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say

Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says

items.title: Atp Finals: media spagnoli, Alcaraz vuole continuare a giocare
items.summary: Il murciano sarebbe determinato a scendere in campo domani con Cobolli
items.content: La volontà di Carlos Alcaraz sarebbe quella di continuare a giocare alle ATP Finals, per cui farà tutto il necessario affinché ciò avvenga. Lo sostengono i media spagnoli, secondo cui il tennista di Murcia, dopo essersi sottoposto a esami medici presso l'Istituto di Medicina Sportiva di Torino, si è convinto a scendere in campo venerdì per disputare l'ultima partita della fase a gironi contro Flavio Cobolli e intenderebbe valutare la situazione giorno per giorno. Ad Alcaraz restano almeno due partite da disputare al torneo dei maestri di Torino: quella irrilevante ai fini della classifica contro il romano e le semifinali di sabato.

items.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
items.summary: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
items.content:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.

The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.

He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.

Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.

While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.

Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.

In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.

The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.

It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.

The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."

Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".

Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".

To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.

Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.

Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.

Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.

However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.

The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.

Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.

He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.

Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.

He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

items.title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
items.summary: This is the second time Smith has requested to be released from prison for killing the two boys, who were both under the age of four at the time.
items.content:
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.

Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.

"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.

The board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.

Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.

According to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, she told the hearing that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex. She also said she was "very, very sorry".

At her last hearing in 2024, her children's father, David Smith, said 30 years in prison was not a severe enough punishment.

"That's only 15 years per child, her own children," he said. "That's just not enough."

Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.

At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."

When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.

Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.

Smith was convicted of murder, but under South Carolina law at the time, she was eligible for a parole hearing every two years after serving 30 years in prison.

In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.

She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

Susan Smith denied parole 30 years after drowning her two sons

items.title: Atp Finals, Shelton supera Jodar in due set. Ora per le semifinali deve tifare Zverev
items.summary: L’americano deve sperare che il numero uno tedesco, già sicuro del primo posto nel girone, vinca almeno un set contro Fils
items.content:
Ben Shelton fa il suo: batte lo spagnolo Rafa Jodar in due set con il punteggio di 7-6 (10-8), 7-5 e agguanta la seconda posizione nel girone delle Atp Finals. Dopo la vittoria all’esordio contro Fils e la sconfitta contro Zverev , l’americano porta a casa quella che è stata fin qui la partita più lunga del torneo, due ore e sei minuti. Ma ancora non è sicuro di prolungare il suo soggiorno a Torino.

Close to the end Shelton grinds out an entertaining first set 7-6(8) against Jodar #NittoATPFinals https://t.co/JWOPC1KJGF

Per andare alle semifinali, il nuovo allievo di Juan Carlos Ferrero , ex coach di Alcaraz , deve tifare per chi lo ha sconfitto, ossia Sascha Zverev. Infatti, Arthur Fils potrebbe strappare il pass a Shelton battendo in due set il numero uno del tennis, già sicuro del primo posto nel girone. In questo caso, l’americano sarebbe penalizzato in classifica per il quoziente di set (+1 contro il +2 del tedesco e del francese). Se invece questa sera Zverev conquistasse almeno un set contro Fils, Shelton approderebbe tra i primi quattro dell’Atp Finals, sfidando il primo classificato dell'altro gruppo.

items.content:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).

Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.

Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)

If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.

We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.

More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).

Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.

How it works…

Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.

When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.

The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.

Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.

This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.

We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.

The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.

We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!

The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

items.title: UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
items.summary: Article URL: https://macanorak.com/uk-government-forced-to-admit-it-issued-apple-a-secret-encryption-order/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50562113 Points: 33 # Comments: 2
items.content:
There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all.

That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 , which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice .

This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat.

I covered the background to this extensively in my piece Two-Tier Encryption in the UK . The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging to users not just in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law.

Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information. [1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services . They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so.

The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice , but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice , this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026 .

The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs.

At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute” .

The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument.

“The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.”

The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret.

In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government.

Alice had enabled advanced data protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users , Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection.

Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature.

Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible.

The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy . Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them.

The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public.

Apple has consistently argued that it will not build ‘backdoors’ into its products. The UK government, meanwhile, has relied on powers that allow it to issue orders to technology companies in secret. For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it.

Advanced Data Protection is not synonymous with all iCloud data encryption. Apple already encrypts various categories of iCloud information without ADP, but some of those categories remain accessible to Apple and can potentially be provided in response to valid legal demands. ADP changes that arrangement by extending end-to-end encryption to additional categories of data. ↩︎

Google Chrome dev team declares bug report bankruptcy [ I wrote this in August 2012 and then forgot about it. ]

About 18 months ago I filed a report for a bug in Google Chrome. It wasn't a very important bug. I reported that when Chrome was asked to inline an image, and the image turned out to be in the obscure and seldom-used X-bitmap format, it came up as a "broken image" icon (which isn't a bug) and failed to display the alt text from the img tag (which is). I then forgot about it until this week, when I got a notice that the report was being closed because it was "obsolete". I was invited to resubmit the bug report if I considered it valid. My first draft of this article continued politely "The Chrome dev team botched this in a number of ways." That draft came out boring, weak, and vague, so I'm going to try continuing a different way. That was a really jerky thing to do. I put in my time and trouble to construct a clear bug report with an easy test case; the bug report contained a link to a page that demonstrated the problem . To see if the problem is still present, all you have to do is click the link in the bug report. But after I spent my time and effort to submit this bug report, Chrome dev decided to ignore it. After they had ignored it for a year and a half, they decided to pitch it in the trash. But if I want, I can submit it again. Now why on earth would I want to do that? Does Chrome think I enjoy assembling bug reports? Maybe I do it for fun? No. The bug report has no value to me. It was an expense. It was a donation to someone I thought would appreciate it. Suppose my neighbor has a boat. Sometimes he lets me use the boat, but it leaks. One day he asks if I will help me fix the boat. I spend the day in his garage painting and sealing some new boards to put into the bottom of the boat. Some time later, I see he has put the new boards into the trash. "What did you do that for?" I ask. He shrugs. "I don't really care if the boat leaks," he says. "But if you want to come over and paint and seal some more boards, how about next week?" Sorry, what am I supposed to get out of this transaction? Chrome dev says they have 40,000 bug reports, too many to deal with. So what? Autoclosing them isn't dealing with them either; it's throwing them in the trash. If having you don't want to get bug reports, yo udon't have to solicit them. They say that a lot of the reports are useless. I'm sure that's true. Most people don't file very good bug reports. A few people do. Who gets pissed off when you throw all the reports into the trash? The people who put in the most effort, that's who. So if you're trying to adopt a strategy that will ensure that your next 40,000 reports are even worse, this is the strategy to adopt. What should Chrome have done here? There is an easy thing and a hard thing. The easy thing not to say "We threw away your report, but if you think it was a good one, please start over and resubmit it," which is likely to piss off anyone with any sense. Instead, you stick a button on the web site and say "We threw away your report, but if you think it was a good one, please click the button." I would not object to checking if the report was still valid, and clicking a button to reactivate it. The harder thing that they should have done was to not close the reports at all. Managing bug reports is hard. Perl was years behind on bug reports for many years. Many of those reports were indeed obsolete. But there is no cost to keeping them around. Addenda A Mastodon colleague was complaining today about a similar practice, and I wanted to refer him to this article, but couldn't because I had completely forgotten to publish it. JWZ complained about something similar in 2003 .

items.title: Il Black Friday Tineco arriva prima. Sconti fino a 250 euro su aspirapolvere e lavapavimenti
items.summary: Cinque prodotti Tineco in promozione fino al 30 novembre, sia su Amazon sia sullo store online. Per il Black Friday inizia a pulire meno e a vivere meglio ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Il Black Friday può essere l'occasione per automatizzare o almeno rendere meno faticose alcune delle attività domestiche che si ripetono ogni giorno. È il principio attorno al quale Tineco, parte del Gruppo ECOVACS, ha costruito la propria selezione di offerte per il Black Friday: cinque prodotti che affrontano esigenze differenti, dalla pulizia quotidiana dei pavimenti alle macchie più difficili, passando per peli di animali, tappeti e tessuti.

Con gli sconti per il Black Friday, validi sia su Amazon sia sullo store online di Tineco, si risparmia fino a 250 euro . Inoltre, acquistando su Amazon è previsto un ulteriore sconto del 6% sul prezzo promozionale Black Friday utilizzando il codice TINECOBFIT in fase dei checkout .

La selezione scelta da Tineco riflette il concetto "Clean Less, Live More" del marchio: usare sensori, automazione, autopulizia e soluzioni meccaniche studiate per ridurre non soltanto il lavoro durante la pulizia, ma anche quello necessario subito dopo.

Dalla possibilità di reclinare a 180° il dispositivo per facilitare il passaggio sotto ai mobili più bassi fino al lavaggio e all’asciugatura automatizzati. Così da passare meno tempo a pulire e più tempo a vivere.

FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Steam Pro è la proposta più completa tra quelle coinvolte nella promozione e nasce per unire in un unico dispositivo aspirazione, lavaggio e trattamento con vapore ad alta temperatura. Ciò per evitare di dover affrontare separatamente polvere, sporco umido e macchie più difficili. Il sistema intelligente, infatti, rileva le condizioni della superficie e modifica automaticamente il funzionamento della lavapavimenti, adattando l'intervento allo sporco incontrato durante il passaggio.

Il vapore aggiunge un'azione specifica quando acqua e aspirazione da sole non sono sufficienti, per esempio nel caso di residui secchi o sporco più aderente al pavimento.

Ma una parte importante del lavoro viene automatizzata anche quando si finisce di pulire. La tecnologia FlashDry gestisce un ciclo di pulizia e asciugatura del rullo , riducendo gli interventi necessari prima di riporre il dispositivo. È disponibile anche un’asciugatura silenziosa che lavora a meno di 45 dB.

La FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Steam Pro Include anche uno schermo facile da avere sempre sott’occhio per conoscere in un attimo l’autonomia residua e la modalità di pulizia selezionata. Mentre il sistema SmoothDrive garantisce una propulsione a 360° e facilita la spinta in ogni direzione, così da non gravare sul polso e ridurre lo sforzo. L’autonomia arriva fino a 90 minuti.

Per il Black Friday, FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Steam Pro è in sconto a 629 euro anziché 849 euro sia su Amazon sia sullo store online di Tineco .

Poco più in basso nella gamma si trova FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Boost Steam. Anche in questo caso il vapore svolge un ruolo da protagonista, ma l’impostazione è più orientata alla rapidità di intervento.

La BoostSteam Technology rende disponibile il getto di vapore in circa 20 secondi alla prima attivazione e in circa 5 secondi per le erogazioni successive. Il vapore può raggiungere una temperatura di 230 °C e viene utilizzato per intervenire su residui secchi e macchie particolarmente ostinate.

A questa azione si affianca la ReverseScrub Technology. La spazzola può ruotare in senso inverso per aumentare l'azione meccanica sul pavimento e raggiungere meglio anche le fughe tra le piastrelle.

L’aspirazione, invece, arriva fino a 25.000 Pa e permette di raccogliere anche lo sporco umido durante il passaggio. Per raggiungere le aree normalmente più difficili c'è il design HyperStretch: la lavapavimenti può reclinarsi fino a 180 gradi e passare così sotto letti, divani e mobili bassi senza obbligare a spostarli. Inoltre, garantisce fino a 60 minuti di autonomia.

Il prezzo di listino di FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Boost Steam è di 699 euro; durante il Black Friday scende a 579,99 euro sia su Amazon sia sul sito ufficiale di Tineco .

FLOOR ONE S7 Stretch Ultra rinuncia al vapore e si concentra, invece, sulla pulizia quotidiana combinando aspirazione e lavaggio in un unico passaggio. Una delle caratteristiche principali è il sistema MHCBS di Tineco, progettato per alimentare continuamente il rullo con acqua pulita e separare quella sporca raccolta durante il passaggio. Il principio è quello di continuare a lavare il pavimento utilizzando un rullo mantenuto pulito durante il funzionamento, anziché trascinare progressivamente lo sporco già raccolto.

Inoltre, per le case nelle quali capelli e peli rappresentano una presenza quotidiana c'è il sistema DualBlock Anti-Tangle, studiato per ridurre la formazione di grovigli attorno al rullo e quindi anche la manutenzione manuale.

La parola "Stretch" anticipa un'altra delle sue caratteristiche distintive: il corpo può reclinarsi completamente fino a 180 gradi, così da lavorare anche sotto mobili e altri elementi bassi senza costringere chi la utilizza a fermarsi o cambiare strumento. In questo modo può passare sotto a mobili alti fino a 13 cm . La posizione reclinata non compromette la qualità della pulizia grazie al sistema di separazione delle acque reflue in tre camere distinte.

È anche uno dei prodotti sui quali il Black Friday incide maggiormente: FLOOR ONE S7 Stretch Ultra passa da un prezzo di listino di 499 euro a 249,99 euro. Lo sconto è attivo sia su Amazon sia sullo store online di Tineco .

Non tutto lo sporco si trova sui pavimenti duri. CARPET ONE Spot DualHeat è pensato proprio per le superfici sulle quali una normale lavapavimenti non può intervenire. Si pensi a tappeti, divani, scale rivestite e sedili o tessuti dell’automobile.

Il sistema combina acqua calda fino a 70 °C e vapore fino a 100 °C . Sono disponibili quattro livelli di pulizia, così da poter calibrare l'intervento in funzione del problema: dallo schizzo appena avvenuto fino allo sporco che ha avuto più tempo per aderire alle fibre.

L'aspirazione arriva fino a 17.000 Pa ed è utilizzata per recuperare l'acqua sporca e i residui dopo il trattamento. Un aspetto particolarmente importante quando si lavano i tessuti è poi il tempo necessario perché tornino utilizzabili: per questo Tineco integra FlipDry, con due modalità di asciugatura pensate proprio per accelerare questa fase. Con questo sistema, il CARPET ONE Spot DualHeat usa l’aria calda fino a 70 °C e un flusso d’aria di 4,2 m/s per asciugare più in fretta. Oppure, in caso di tessuti sensibili al calore, come tappeti in lana e biancheria in cotone, si può optare per un’asciugatura più delicata.

CARPET ONE Spot DualHeat ha un prezzo di listino di 249 euro e per il Black Friday viene proposto a 209 euro. La promozione è disponibile sia su Amazon sia sul sito di Tineco .

PURE ONE S50 Pro Pet è il prodotto più accessibile della selezione Black Friday, ma anche quello con un compito molto specifico: semplificare la pulizia quotidiana nelle abitazioni in cui vivono cani e gatti. In queste case il problema non è necessariamente lo sporco più difficile, quanto la sua frequenza. Peli, capelli e polvere ricompaiono continuamente e richiedono quindi uno strumento che possa essere utilizzato rapidamente senza trasformare ogni passaggio in una sessione di pulizia completa.

Per questo PURE ONE S50 Pro Pet utilizza una spazzola anti-groviglio progettata per raccogliere capelli e peli limitandone l'accumulo sulla spazzola stessa. Una volta finito, anche lo svuotamento del contenitore avviene con un solo gesto.

Prima ancora di aspirare, però, bisogna riuscire a vedere lo sporco. Il faro verde grandangolare copre un angolo di 120 gradi e mette in evidenza particelle fino a 0,02 mm, comprese quelle che possono risultare poco visibili a occhio nudo sul pavimento.

Il sensore iLoop, invece, lavora durante l'aspirazione: rileva quanto sporco è presente e modifica automaticamente la potenza, evitando di dover regolare continuamente il dispositivo a mano e contribuendo a gestire meglio la carica disponibile. L'autonomia dichiarata arriva fino a 90 minuti , mentre il design reclinabile aiuta a passare sotto mobili e arredi bassi, dove peli e polvere tendono facilmente ad accumularsi.

PURE ONE S50 Pro Pet è in promozione su Amazon e sullo store online di Tineco fino al 30 novembre a 199 euro, rispetto al prezzo precedente di 299 euro

items.title: Attacchi informatici con lAI in meno di tre ore, lallarme FBI
items.summary: LFBI documenta intrusioni accelerate dallIA e avverte le aziende sui tempi di risposta.
items.content:
Tre ore sono davvero poche se ci pensiamo, ma in alcuni casi descritti dall'FBI sono bastate per arrivare a un accesso con privilegi elevati, cioè con permessi che consentono di intervenire su parti del sistema normalmente riservate agli amministratori. A rendere più rapidi quegli attacchi è stato ARTEX, un programma ideato per mettere alla prova le difese informatiche con l'autorizzazione delle aziende.

La segnalazione dell'FBI risale al 13 novembre e raccoglie episodi osservati almeno da agosto. Tra i bersagli ci sono banche, enti governativi e società tecnologiche, con effetti che cambiano parecchio da caso a caso. Per le campagne contro il settore finanziario sudcoreano l'FBI stima circa 67.000 persone a cui sono state sottratte informazioni personali. Nella vicenda ConnectWise Cloud Backup, i più di 2.250 ambienti cloud citati nel bollettino sono quelli verso cui sono stati osservati tentativi di accesso.

Barracuda ha raccontato un'altra conseguenza, che riguarda il lavoro di chi deve ricostruire l'incidente. La società aveva ancora attiva una credenziale legata a un rapporto con un fornitore ormai concluso, ma dopo aver scoperto cosa era successo, ha dovuto sostituire le credenziali interessate perché dai registri disponibili era impossibile stabilire con certezza quali fossero state consultate.

items.title: Liberty Media potrebbe vendere la F1 e la MotoGP, l'incredibile indiscrezione
items.summary: L'ex CEO di Liberty Media Greg Maffei ha considerato l'uscita dalla Borsa e la cessione della Formula 1 entro 2 anni.
items.content:
L'acquisizione della Formula 1 da parte degli americani di Liberty Media è stata annunciata a settembre 2016 e completata a gennaio 2017, rilevando la massima categoria del Motorsport dal fondo CVC Capital Partners. L'exit di Bernie Ecclestone ha stravolto le logiche del campionato con una visione orientata all'accrescimento di un nuovo audience, principalmente tramite una visibilità che è passata attraverso i social media e Netflix.Greg Maffei, ex Presidente e CEO di Liberty Media sino al 2024, ha avuto la possibilità di gestire i conti del circus e, nel corso della conferenza Sportico's Invest New York 2026, ha rappresentato uno scenario sorprendente: entro i prossimi 2 anni la Formula 1 potrebbe uscire dalla Borsa per finire per essere ceduta a una nuova proprietà. Questo lascerebbe pensare che tutti gli investimenti fatti, proiettati anche all'aumento dei capitali, siano frutto di una strategia ben precisa, focalizzata a una futura vendita.

Voci di corridoio

Per ora Liberty Media non ha smentito ma nemmeno confermato i rumor. C'è chi conosce meglio di altri i fili che muovono il circus e gli obblighi fiduciari di un consiglio di amministrazione nei confronti dei propri azionisti. Con l'offerta giusta per Liberty Media sarebbe difficile rinunciare all'idea di una futura cessione in una fase in cui i numeri sono all'apice. Quando Liberty Media acquistò i diritti commerciali della Formula 1 da CVC Capital Partners, l'operazione fu valutata intorno ai 4,6 miliardi di dollari, circa 4,1 miliardi di euro.Grazie a una crescita su diversi mercati, complice anche il successo di Drive To Survive, la popolarità dei protagonisti del circus è esplosa. Il titolo in Borsa è cresciuto di circa il 250% e l'EBITDA, ovvero il margine operativo lordo, è triplicato nel giro di otto o nove anni. La F1 sarà ancora quotata sul mercato azionario nel 2028? Per Maffei potrebbe già aver cambiato proprietario. In sostanza i risultati finanziari più importanti sono già stati raggiunti e triplicare nuovamente la redditività nei prossimi otto o nove anni, partendo da una base che oggi sfiora indicativamente i 28-30 miliardi di dollari di valutazione complessiva, appare una missione impossibile persino per la proprietà americana.[caption id="attachment_293942" align="alignnone" width="1200"] Il team Cadillac di F1 è in vendita[/caption]

Cosa sta accadendo

Il fondatore John Malone, dirigente d'azienda e noto per il suo ruolo nella televisione via cavo e nei media, ha rivalutato il proprio potere di voto all'interno di Liberty Media, scendendo dal 48% a circa il 3%. Riducendo la concentrazione dei diritti di voto, il magnate ha lasciato al consiglio di amministrazione un ruolo centrale nella valutazione di eventuali operazioni straordinarie. Le future proposte dovranno essere giudicate con un assetto di governance profondamente diversa, ma l'ultima parola l'avrà sempre la FIA.Liberty Media ha ottenuto da Dorna Sports anche la MotoGP, nel 2025, con un'operazione dal valore d'impresa stimato intorno ai 4,3 miliardi di euro. In caso di passo indietro sulla F1, anche la MotoGP risulterebbe coinvolta. Per ora c'è l'obiettivo di accrescere l'audience sul campionato, allargarne il pubblico globale e aumentarne l'appeal commerciale. Una strategia che riprende alcuni degli strumenti già sfruttati con il circus della F1, ma qualora il valore dovesse moltiplicarsi, anche la top class del Motomondiale potrebbe essere ceduta a un fondo d'investimento o a un grande gruppo dell'intrattenimento.

items.title: Google Foto potrebbe suggerire come abbinare i vestiti
items.summary: Nellapp Google Foto spuntano tracce di una funzione per suggerire abbinamenti.
items.content:
Google Foto potrebbe cominciare a suggerire come abbinare i vestiti che riconosce nelle nostre foto, stando a quanto scoperto da Android Authority.

La testata ha trovato nella versione 8.2 dell'app alcune voci dedicate a una funzione chiamata «Build a fit». Una delle opzioni, «Surprise me», fa pensare a un pulsante per lasciare all'app la scelta dei capi, ma chi ha esaminato il codice non è riuscito ad attivare la funzione, quindi per ora ci sono solo le tracce nell'app.

La novità si innesterebbe su Wardrobe, il guardaroba digitale arrivato in Google Foto. L'app riconosce i vestiti indossati nelle immagini della raccolta e li raduna in una sezione dove si possono ritrovare, per esempio, tutte le maglie o i pantaloni. Oggi la combinazione si fa a mano, scegliendo fino a sei pezzi alla volta, e si possono poi provare i capi virtualmente o salvare gli abbinamenti per ritrovarli più avanti.

items.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
items.summary: At least four bodies have been recovered from the boat which was reportedly carrying between 50 and 100 people.
items.content:
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.

Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.

This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).

"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.

A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.

However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.

Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.

He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.

Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.

Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.

The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.

It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.

As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.

They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.

Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.

They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.

On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.

It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

items.title: Comincia il Black Friday Amazon: tutte le migliori offerte tech, in continuo aggiornamento
items.summary: I migliori prodotti in sconto: TV, smartphone, robot aspirapolvere, videogiochi e altro ancora ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Il Black Friday si sta avvicinando e Amazon ha preparato oltre dieci giorni di sconti e promozioni.

Fino alle 23.59 del 30 novembre, tutti gli utenti - anche se non abbonati ad Amazon Prime - potranno usufruire di tantissimi sconti su ogni genere di prodotti: TV, monitor, lavatrici, smartphone, console, rasoi, videocamere di sorveglianza e tanto altro.

Anche quest'anno la redazione di DDAY ha deciso di raccogliere in un unico articolo tutte le migliori occasioni del Black Friday Amazon, per poter agevolare la fruizione e fornire un unico grande articolo di riferimento.

Sarà continuamente aggiornato per segnalare ogni possibile offerta sull'elettronica di consumo.

Su DDeals , il portale delle offerte di DDAY.it, saranno accessibili le migliori offerte sui prodotti di tecnologia: TV, robot aspirapolvere, console da gioco, smartphone e altro ancora.

La scopa elettrica H15 Pro di Dreame è in offerta per il Black Friday Amazon a 299 euro .

Mentre il robot aspirapolvere lavapavimenti DREAME L60 Ultra CE è scontato a 499 euro .

Anche Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow è in offerta al prezzo di 349euro.

E la Nescafè Dolce Gusto è in offerta al prezzo più basso di sempre di 66,40 euro.

Anche la friggitrice ad aria verticale Philips Airfryer 4000 è ora in offerta a 159,99 euro.

La cantinetta vino Haier da 30 bottiglie è ora in offerta a 246 euro.

Fra le videocamere di sorveglianza, segnaliamo le offerte sulle Arlo Ultra 3, anche con Smarthub incluso e in kit con più unità.

items.title: Da USB a WiFi: vecchia stampante torna a nuova vita con Raspberry e pochi euro
items.summary: + CUPS. Risultato: niente più cavi
items.content:
Recuperare una stampante USB vecchia di 7 anni tramite un piccolo computer, un Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W da meno di 20 euro e il software gratuito CUPS. Non è semplicemente un'idea "geniale", ma il piano messo in atto e ben riuscito da Abhishek Kumar Mishra, autore di XDA Developers.

Proprio su XDA, Mishra ha descritto nel dettaglio tutti i passaggi. Anzitutto, la stampante in questione è una Canon PIXMA MG2577S, "in uso sin dai tempi dell'università". Di per sé, il modello funzionava ancora alla grande, ma c'era un piccolo problema nell'utilizzo pratico di tutti i giorni. Per stampare, infatti, bisognava collegarla fisicamente al computer, liberando una porta USB e interrompendo il normale lavoro. Inoltre, anche gli altri componenti della famiglia - lontani dalla postazione desktop - avevano bisogno di utilizzarla.

Da qui lo sviluppo di una soluzione e del progetto vero e proprio: sfruttare un Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, più altri 3 componenti software, per trasformarla in stampante Wi-Fi.

Il miglior smartphone pieghevole del momento? Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 7, compralo al miglior prezzo da Productpine.com a 622 euro.

items.title: Why AI Wants to Be Local – With Pete Warden (Creator of Moonshine Voice)
items.summary: Article URL: https://thedataexchange.media/pete-warden-moonshine/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50561508 Points: 78 # Comments: 53
items.content:
Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS .

Pete Warden , co-creator of Moonshine Voice and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World , a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.]

Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast.

Ben Lorica. All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI?

Pete Warden. Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models.

That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model.

That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models.

Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available.

Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for.

What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives.

I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me.

As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for.

Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt?

Pete Warden. So a lot of it comes down to your model choice.

Pete Warden. You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives.

Ben Lorica. But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small?

Pete Warden. So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that.

But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them.

So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory.

Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed.

Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other.

Ben Lorica. So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it.

Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there?

For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work?

Pete Warden. I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement.

Ben Lorica. But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete.

Pete Warden. I think the biggest barriers are usability. If you look at the benchmarks, it really is no longer a question of model quality.

Pete Warden. Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut.

And people are finding that some of the models actually work better, especially if you’re dealing with things like, I don’t want to call it censorship because I feel like that’s a loaded term, but a lot of commercial models have restrictions. They may be intended to prevent a bad use case, but pretty often they can also trip you up even if you’re trying to do something benign.

I know a lot of people who work in cybersecurity, for example, who are white hats, but they’re having to work with a lot of stuff where they’re asking questions about malicious actions. With the commercial models, you’re going to keep tripping over the restrictions and the guardrails that are built in with good intentions, but they can really impact your work.

Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. By the way, Pete, the model is one component, but then there are the things surrounding the model, the so-called harness, or even context, memory, knowledge.

items.title: Show HN: Watch weight-space programming in action with WebGPU
items.summary: I wanted to build a full weight-space programming loop entirely in the browser with WebGPU: let an LLM inspect Qwen3.5-0.8B, edit its weights, evaluate, and repeat. the full loop needed too much VRAM. so I turned it into an interactive walkthrough of a concrete example: editing 0.016% of a model's weights to reduce reasoning loops, no gradient descent. Based on exp8 of “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming.”: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50341174 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50561436 Points: 5 # Comments: 1
items.content:
A real recording of both models on the same prompt with the same seed. It plays by itself — drag the timeline, change the speed, or pick another case.

Fetching the recorded token streams (about 1 MB). Everything else on the page already works.

Press play. Thinking text appears in grey, the final answer in dark ink.

Press play. Thinking text appears in grey, the final answer in dark ink.

The replay cases come from a batch of MATH-500 problems recorded with the same settings.

With thinking on, small Qwen keeps re-checking itself — “wait, let me verify…” — until it runs out of budget instead of answering.

It subtracts one direction from 64 neurons' output weights ( ffn_down ) in layers 15 and 19 — 131,072 of ~800M weights.

Stripes drawn ~25× wider than true scale — at real size they would be invisible.

Same model, same prompts — it now stops looping and finishes its answers.

Model souping - diffusion-LoRA merging is one case of it - is weight-space editing too. The difference is the target: souping picks merge weights (and sometimes merge order) with a broad benchmark; weight-space programming zeroes in on a few specific failure cases and the neurons behind them. And here's the fun part: it's a promising fit for agents - propose an edit, test it, feed the result back - the same edit-test-repeat loop behind the recent coding-agent wins.

Where the 131,072 changed weights sit, and what the edited neurons do while the model thinks.

Which of the 3,584 neurons feeding each edited ffn_down tensor were changed, and by how much.

The 64 edited neurons of layers 15 and 19, token by token, on the recorded runs. Synced to the replay above: hover to peek, drag to scrub.

how hard the edit pushes · |push| per token · L15: the dashed line equals base by construction (layers below 15 are unchanged)

n = 4 loops + 1 control · correlation, not proof · bf16 forward over the recorded tokens · int8-quantised for the web

Footnote: the recorder marks only non-overlapping repeats, so a loop can start later than the text actually repeats; your browser re-checks every repeat and hatches the missed part. “Push” is what the edit would add given the base activations — its sign is a convention, so the chart shows its size.

Both models run locally via llama.cpp → WebAssembly + WebGPU. Nothing is sent to a server.

Sequential runs unload each model by default to limit GPU memory. n_ctx / n_gpu_layers apply on the next load.

How long each model talks, and how it ends: grey = thinking, colour = answer, ✓ = stopped on its own, ⚠ = hit the cap. x = stream chunk (≈ one token).

items.title: Telemarketing vietato in ogni settore, la proposta arriva alla Camera
items.summary: Due emendamenti al DDL Concorrenza cancellerebbero anche le eccezioni oggi previste per luce e gas. Altre tre proposte vorrebbero estendere il divieto solo agli operatori telefonici ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Due emendamenti presentati alla Camera hanno proposto di vietare le telefonate e i messaggi commerciali per qualsiasi prodotto o servizio e non più soltanto per i contratti di luce e gas. Li hanno firmati deputati della Lega (Luca Toccalini, Giorgia Andreuzza e Salvatore Marcello Di Mattina) e di Forza Italia (Luca Squeri e Giorgio Lovecchio), e riguardano il DDL Concorrenza 2026, che è all’esame della commissione Attività produttive.

I due testi andrebbero a riscrivere le regole dell’articolo 51 del Codice del consumo che dal 19 giugno vietano le sollecitazioni telefoniche per le sole forniture di energia . Il nuovo divieto scatterebbe 60 giorni dopo l’entrata in vigore e cancellerebbe le due eccezioni attuali , cioè quelle che permettono a un fornitore di energia di fare telemarketing:

Cambierebbe anche il caso in cui AGCOM può far sospendere le linee telefoniche. Oggi può farlo solo se l’azienda chiama da un numero diverso da quello che la identifica ; con gli emendamenti basterebbe una qualsiasi violazione del divieto, anche una chiamata partita dal numero ufficiale, per bloccare le linee da cui l’azienda telefona.

Altre tre proposte vorrebbero estendere il divieto attuale ai servizi di telecomunicazione . Le hanno firmate di nuovo i tre deputati leghisti, Mauro Del Barba di Italia Viva ed Eliana Longi e Fabio Pietrella di Fratelli d’Italia.

Tutte e tre allargherebbero l’eccezione per i clienti consenzienti, oggi limitata a quelli di luce e gas, a tutti i clienti dell’azienda, e le versioni di Lega e Italia Viva anche ai clienti di altre società dello stesso gruppo.

Facciamo chiarezza, perché capiamo che la materia può essere ostica:

È il terzo tentativo dell’anno di estendere il divieto alle telecomunicazioni . A maggio gli emendamenti al decreto Fiscale erano stati ritirati o respinti, mentre a giugno l’estensione era passata in commissione al Senato con il decreto Accise ed era poi stata stralciata alla Camera.

Il motivo è un’asimmetria delle regole attuali che è stata segnalata a settembre anche dall’Antitrust : un fornitore di energia può chiamare i propri clienti per proporre offerte di telefonia, mentre un operatore telefonico che vende anche luce e gas non può chiamare i suoi clienti di telefonia per proporre energia, nemmeno con il loro consenso .

Le tre proposte sulle telecomunicazioni toccano proprio questo punto, perché l’eccezione varrebbe per tutti i clienti dell’azienda. L’Antitrust aveva però avvertito che la sola estensione agli operatori telefonici potrebbe non bastare a correggere tutti gli squilibri concorrenziali delle regole attuali .

A quella segnalazione si richiama anche la memoria con cui Assocall, l’associazione dei call center di Confcommercio, il sindacato UGL Terziario e alcune associazioni di consumatori, tra cui Codacons e Assoutenti, hanno chiesto di rivedere tutti e cinque gli emendamenti.

In ogni caso gli emendamenti sono ancora tali, e dovranno passare il vaglio della commissione prima di arrivare in Aula .

items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
items.summary: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
items.content:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

While in China, Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".

Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls

The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.

Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".

Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.

Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.

"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."

Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".

It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."

Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.

He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".

Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".

He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.

As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.

Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.

In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.

There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.

The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.

"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.

"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."

The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.

"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."

Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.

It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".

Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.

Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.

The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
